They include increases in the frequency and intensity of hot extremes, marine heatwaves, heavy precipitation, and, in some regions, agricultural and ecological droughts; an increase in the proportion of intense tropical cyclones; and reductions in Arctic sea ice, snow cover and permafrost.</span> <span class="readmore btn-primary btn-ipcc">Expand</span><span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-5"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figures SPM.5</a>, <a href="#figure-spm-6">SPM.6</a>, <a href="#figure-spm-8">SPM.8</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 4.5, 4.6, 7.4, 8.2, 8.4, Box 8.2, 9.3, 9.5, Box 9.2, 11.1, 11.2, 11.3, 11.4, 11.6, 11.7, 11.9, Cross-Chapter Box 11.1, 12.4, 12.5, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, Atlas.4, Atlas.5, Atlas.6, Atlas.7, Atlas.8, Atlas.9, Atlas.10, Atlas.11</span></span></p><div class="spmbulletcont" id="spmbulletcont-b2"><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.2.1</span> It is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">virtually certain</i> that the land surface will continue to warm more than the ocean surface (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i>1.4 to 1.7 times more). It is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">virtually certain</i> that the Arctic will continue to warm more than global surface temperature, with <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i> above two times the rate of global warming.   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">2.3, 4.3, 4.5, 4.6, 7.4, 11.1, 11.3, 11.9, 12.4, 12.5, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, Atlas.4, Atlas.5, Atlas.6, Atlas.7, Atlas.8, Atlas.9, Atlas.10, Atlas.11, Cross-Section Box TS.1, TS.2.6</span></span> <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-5"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.5</a></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.2.2</span> With every additional increment of global warming, changes in extremes continue to become larger. For example, every additional 0.5°C of global warming causes clearly discernible increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes, including heatwaves (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely</i>) , and heavy precipitation (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>), as well as agricultural and ecological droughts<sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-019-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-019">30</a></span></sup> in some regions (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Discernible changes in intensity and frequency of meteorological droughts, with more regions showing increases than decreases, are seen in some regions for every additional 0.5°C of global warming (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). Increases in frequency and intensity of hydrological droughts become larger with increasing global warming in some regions (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). There will be an increasing occurrence of some extreme events unprecedented in the observational record with additional global warming, even at 1.5°C of global warming. Projected percentage changes in frequency are larger for rarer events (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">8.2, 11.2, 11.3, 11.4, 11.6, 11.9, Cross-Chapter Box 11.1, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, TS.2.6</span></span> <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-5"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.5</a> <a href="#figure-spm-6"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.6</a></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.2.3</span> Some mid-latitude and semi-arid regions, and the South American Monsoon region, are projected to see the highest increase in the temperature of the hottest days, at about 1.5 to 2 times the rate of global warming (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). The Arctic is projected to experience the highest increase in the temperature of the coldest days, at about three times the rate of global warming (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). With additional global warming, the frequency of marine heatwaves will continue to increase (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>), particularly in the tropical ocean and the Arctic (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">Box 9.2, 11.1, 11.3, 11.9, Cross-Chapter Box 11.1, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, 12.4, TS.2.4, TS.2.6</span></span> <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-6"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.6</a></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.2.4</span> It is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i> that heavy precipitation events will intensify and become more frequent in most regions with additional global warming. At the global scale, extreme daily precipitation events are projected to intensify by about 7% for each 1°C of global warming (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). The proportion of intense tropical cyclones (Category 4–5) and peak wind speeds of the most intense tropical cyclones are projected to increase at the global scale with increasing global warming (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">8.2, 11.4, 11.7, 11.9, Cross-Chapter Box 11.1, Box TS.6, TS.4.3.1</span></span> <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-5"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.5</a> <a href="#figure-spm-6"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.6</a></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.2.5</span> Additional warming is projected to further amplify permafrost thawing and loss of seasonal snow cover, of land ice and of Arctic sea ice (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). The Arctic is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i> to be practically sea ice-free in September<sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-018-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-018">31</a></span></sup> at least once before 2050 under the five illustrative scenarios considered in this report, with more frequent occurrences for higher warming levels. The local (i.e., grid point) observed annual mean surface temperature changes are linearly regressed against the global surface temperature in the period 1850–2020. Observed temperature data are from Berkeley Earth, the dataset with the largest coverage and highest horizontal resolution. Linear regression is applied to all years for which data at the corresponding grid point is available. The regression method was used to take into account the complete observational time series and thereby reduce the role of internal variability at the grid point level. White indicates areas where time coverage was 100 years or less and thereby too short to calculate a reliable linear regression. The <span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-"> right map </span> is based on model simulations and shows change in annual multi-model mean simulated temperatures at a global warming level of 1°C (20-year mean global surface temperature change relative to 1850–1900). The triangles at each end of the colour bar indicate out-of-bound values, that is, values above or below the given limits.</p><p class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-table-note---no-title" lang="en-US"><span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-">Panel (b) Simulated annual mean temperature change (°C), panel (c) precipitation change (%), and panel (d) total column soil moisture change (standard deviation of interannual variability) </span> at global warming levels of 1.5°C, 2°C and 4°C (20-year mean global surface temperature change relative to 1850–1900). Simulated changes correspond to Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) multi-model mean change (median change for soil moisture) at the corresponding global warming level, that is, the same method as for the right map in panel (a).</p><p class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-table-note---no-title" lang="en-US">In<span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-"> panel (c)</span>, high positive percentage changes in dry regions may correspond to small absolute changes. In<span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-"> panel (d)</span>, the unit is the standard deviation of interannual variability in soil moisture during 1850–1900. Standard deviation is a widely used metric in characterizing drought severity. A projected reduction in mean soil moisture by one standard deviation corresponds to soil moisture conditions typical of droughts that occurred about once every six years during 1850–1900. In panel (d), large changes in dry regions with little interannual variability in the baseline conditions can correspond to small absolute change. The triangles at each end of the colour bars indicate out-of-bound values, that is, values above or below the given limits. Results from all models reaching the corresponding warming level in any of the five illustrative scenarios (SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5) are averaged. Maps of annual mean temperature and precipitation changes at a global warming level of 3°C are available in Figure 4.31 and Figure 4.32 in <a class="section-link" data-title="Implications of Climate Policy" href="/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-4#4.6">Section 4.6</a><i class="•-Condensed-italic">. </i>Corresponding maps of panels (b), (c) and (d), including hatching to indicate the level of model agreement at grid-cell level, are found in Figures 4.31, 4.32 and 11.19, respectively; as highlighted in Cross-Chapter Box Atlas.1, grid-cell level hatching is not informative for larger spatial scales (e.g., over AR6 reference regions) where the aggregated signals are less affected by small-scale variability, leading to an increase in robustness.   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure 1.14, 4.6.1, Cross-Chapter Box 11.1, Cross-Chapter Box Atlas.1, TS.1.3.2, Figures TS.3 and TS.5</span></span></p><div class="ch-figure-button-cont"><a href="/report/ar6/wg1/figures/summary-for-policymakers/figure-spm-5" target="_blank"><button class="btn-ipcc btn btn-primary ch-figure-button">Open figure</button></a></div></div><div class="_idGenObjectLayout-1 Body-copy_Boxes_Blue-Boxes_•-Box-extract" id="figure-spm-6"><div class="•-2-column-graphic" id="_idContainer009"><img loading="lazy" alt="" class="_idGenObjectAttribute-1" src="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/figures/IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM_Figure_6.png"/><strong class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-title--bold-to-------spans-columns" lang="en-US"><span class="•-Figure-table-number---title"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/>  </span><span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-">Figure SPM.6 | Projected changes in the intensity and frequency of hot temperature extremes over land, extreme precipitation over land, and agricultural and ecological droughts in drying regions</span></strong><p class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-table-note---no-title" lang="en-US">Projected changes are shown at global warming levels of 1°C, 1.5°C, 2°C, and 4°C and are relative to 1850–1900, <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-040-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-040">9</a></span></sup>representing a climate without human influence. The figure depicts frequencies and increases in intensity of 10- or 50-year extreme events from the base period (1850–1900) under different global warming levels.</p><p class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-table-note---no-title" lang="en-US"><span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-">Hot temperature extremes</span> are defined as the daily maximum temperatures over land that were exceeded on average once in a decade (10-year event) or once in 50 years (50-year event) during the 1850–1900 reference period. <span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-">Extreme precipitation events</span><span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-"></span> are defined as the daily precipitation amount over land that was exceeded on average once in a decade during the 1850–1900 reference period. <span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-">Agricultural and ecological drought events</span> are defined as the annual average of total column soil moisture below the 10th percentile of the 1850–1900 base period. These extremes are defined on model grid box scale. For hot temperature extremes and extreme precipitation, results are shown for the global land. For agricultural and ecological drought, results are shown for drying regions only, which correspond to the AR6 regions in which there is at least <i class="•-Light-condensed-italic">medium confidence</i> in a projected increase in agricultural and ecological droughts at the 2°C warming level compared to the 1850–1900 base period in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). These regions include Western North America, Central North America, Northern Central America, Southern Central America, Caribbean, Northern South America, North-Eastern South America, South American Monsoon, South-Western South America, Southern South America, Western and Central Europe, Mediterranean, West Southern Africa, East Southern Africa, Madagascar, Eastern Australia, and Southern Australia (Caribbean is not included in the calculation of the figure because of the too-small number of full land grid cells). The non-drying regions do not show an overall increase or decrease in drought severity. Projections of changes in agricultural and ecological droughts in the CMIP Phase 5 (CMIP5) multi-model ensemble differ from those in CMIP6 in some regions, including in parts of Africa and Asia. Assessments of projected changes in meteorological and hydrological droughts are provided in Chapter 11.</p><p class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-table-note---no-title" lang="en-US">In the <span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-">‘frequency’ section</span>, each year is represented by a dot. The dark dots indicate years in which the extreme threshold is exceeded, while light dots are years when the threshold is not exceeded. Values correspond to the medians (in bold) and their respective <i class="•-Condensed-italic"></i>5–95% range based on the multi-model ensemble from simulations of CMIP6 under different Shared Socio-economic Pathway scenarios. For consistency, the number of dark dots is based on the rounded-up median. In The <span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-">‘intensity’ section</span>, medians and their 5–95% range, also based on the multi-model ensemble from simulations of CMIP6, are displayed as dark and light bars, respectively. Changes in the intensity of hot temperature extremes and extreme precipitation are expressed as degree Celsius and percentage. As for agricultural and ecological drought, intensity changes are expressed as fractions of standard deviation of annual soil moisture.   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">11.1; 11.3; 11.4; 11.6; 11.9; Figures 11.12, 11.15, 11.6, 11.7, and 11.18</span></span></p><div class="ch-figure-button-cont"><a href="/report/ar6/wg1/figures/summary-for-policymakers/figure-spm-6" target="_blank"><button class="btn-ipcc btn btn-primary ch-figure-button">Open figure</button></a></div></div></div></div><p id="readmore-b3" class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify--all-bold--BLUE--No-space-below readmore"><span class="bulletnum">B.3</span> <span class="readmore bullet-title">Continued global warming is projected to further intensify the global water cycle, including its variability, global monsoon precipitation and the severity of wet and dry events.</span>      <span class="readmore btn-primary btn-ipcc">Expand</span><span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-5"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figures SPM.5</a>, <a href="#figure-spm-6">SPM.6</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6, 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, 8.5, Box 8.2, 11.4, 11.6, 11.9, 12.4, Atlas.3</span></span></p><div class="spmbulletcont" id="spmbulletcont-b3"><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.3.1</span> There is strengthened evidence since AR5 that the global water cycle will continue to intensify as global temperatures rise (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>), with precipitation and surface water flows projected to become more variable over most land regions within seasons (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>) and from year to year (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). The average annual global land precipitation is projected to increase by 0–5% under the very low GHG emissions scenario (SSP1-1.9), 1.5–8% for the intermediate GHG emissions scenario (SSP2-4.5) and 1–13% under the very high GHG emissions scenario (SSP5-8.5) by 2081–2100 relative to 1995–2014 (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i>ranges). Precipitation is projected to increase over high latitudes, the equatorial Pacific and parts of the monsoon regions, but decrease over parts of the subtropics and limited areas in the tropics in SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5 (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely</i>) . The portion of the global land experiencing detectable increases or decreases in seasonal mean precipitation is projected to increase (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). There is <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i> in an earlier onset of spring snowmelt, with higher peak flows at the expense of summer flows in snow-dominated regions globally.   <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-5"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.5</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 4.5, 4.6, 8.2, 8.4, Atlas.3, TS.2.6, TS.4.3, Box TS.6</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.3.2</span> A warmer climate will intensify very wet and very dry weather and climate events and seasons, with implications for flooding or drought (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>), but the location and frequency of these events depend on projected changes in regional atmospheric circulation, including monsoons and mid-latitude storm tracks. It is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i> that rainfall variability related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation is projected to be amplified by the second half of the 21st century in the SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios.  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-5"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.5</a> <a href="#figure-spm-6"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.6</a></span> <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 4.5, 4.6, 8.2, 8.4, 8.5, 11.4, 11.6, 11.9, 12.4, TS.2.6, TS.4.2, Box TS.6</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.3.3</span> Monsoon precipitation is projected to increase in the mid- to long term at the global scale, particularly over South and South East Asia, East Asia and West Africa apart from the far west Sahel (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). The monsoon season is projected to have a delayed onset over North and South America and West Africa (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>) and a delayed retreat over West Africa (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.4, 4.5, 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, Box 8.2, Box TS.13</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.3.4</span> A projected southward shift and intensification of Southern Hemisphere summer mid-latitude storm tracks and associated precipitation is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i> in the long term under high GHG emissions scenarios (SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5), but in the near term the effect of stratospheric ozone recovery counteracts these changes (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). There is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i> in a continued poleward shift of storms and their precipitation in the North Pacific, while there is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">low confidence</i> in projected changes in the North Atlantic storm tracks.   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.4, 4.5, 8.4, TS.2.3, TS.4.2</span></span></p></div><p id="readmore-b4" class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify--all-bold--BLUE--No-space-below readmore"><span class="bulletnum">B.4</span> <span class="readmore bullet-title">Under scenarios with increasing CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions, the ocean and land carbon sinks are projected to be less effective at slowing the accumulation of CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> in the atmosphere.</span> <span class="readmore btn-primary btn-ipcc">Expand</span><span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-7"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.7</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 5.2, 5.4, 5.5, 5.6</span></span></p><div class="spmbulletcont" id="spmbulletcont-b4"><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.4.1</span> While natural land and ocean carbon sinks are projected to take up, in absolute terms, a progressively larger amount of CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> under higher compared to lower CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions scenarios, they become less effective, that is, the proportion of emissions taken up by land and ocean decrease with increasing cumulative CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions. This is projected to result in a higher proportion of emitted CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> remaining in the atmosphere (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-7"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.7</a></span> <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">5.2, 5.4, Box TS.5</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.4.2</span> Based on model projections, under the intermediate GHG emissions scenario that stabilizes atmospheric CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> concentrations this century (SSP2-4.5), the rates of CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> taken up by the land and ocean are projected to decrease in the second half of the 21st century (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Under the very low and low GHG emissions scenarios (SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6), where CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> concentrations peak and decline during the 21st century, the land and ocean begin to take up less carbon in response to declining atmospheric CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> concentrations (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>) and turn into a weak net source by 2100 under SSP1-1.9 (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). It is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very unlikely </i> that the combined global land and ocean sink will turn into a source by 2100 under scenarios without net negative emissions (SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5). <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-017-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-017">32</a></span></sup>      <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 5.4, 5.5, 5.6, Box TS.5, TS.3.3</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.4.3</span> The magnitude of feedbacks between climate change and the carbon cycle becomes larger but also more uncertain in high CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions scenarios (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">very high confidence</i>). However, climate model projections show that the uncertainties in atmospheric CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> concentrations by 2100 are dominated by the differences between emissions scenarios (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Additional ecosystem responses to warming not yet fully included in climate models, such as CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> and CH<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">4</sub> fluxes from wetlands, permafrost thaw and wildfires, would further increase concentrations of these gases in the atmosphere (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">5.4, Box TS.5, TS.3.2</span></span></p><div class="_idGenObjectLayout-1 Body-copy_Boxes_Blue-Boxes_•-Box-extract" id="figure-spm-7"><div class="•-2-column-graphic" id="_idContainer010"><img loading="lazy" alt="" class="_idGenObjectAttribute-1" src="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/figures/IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM_Figure_7.png"/><strong class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-title--bold-to-------spans-columns---Notes-below" lang="en-US"><span class="•-Figure-table-number---title"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.7 | </span>Cumulative anthropogenic CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions taken up by land and ocean sinks by 2100 under the five illustrative scenarios</strong><p class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-table-note---no-title" lang="en-US">The cumulative anthropogenic (human-caused) carbon dioxide (CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub>) emissions taken up by the land and ocean sinks under the five illustrative scenarios (SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5) are simulated from 1850 to 2100 by Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) climate models in the concentration-driven simulations. Land and ocean carbon sinks respond to past, current and future emissions; therefore, cumulative sinks from 1850 to 2100 are presented here. During the historical period (1850–2019) the observed land and ocean sink took up 1430 GtCO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> (59% of the emissions).</p><p class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-table-note---no-title" lang="en-US"><span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-">The bar chart </span>illustrates the projected amount of cumulative anthropogenic CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions (GtCO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub>) between 1850 and 2100 remaining in the atmosphere (grey part) and taken up by the land and ocean (coloured part) in the year 2100. <span class="•-Bold-condensed--dark-blue-">The doughnut chart </span>illustrates the proportion of the cumulative anthropogenic CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions taken up by the land and ocean sinks and remaining in the atmosphere in the year 2100. Values in % indicate the proportion of the cumulative anthropogenic CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions taken up by the combined land and ocean sinks in the year 2100. The overall anthropogenic carbon emissions are calculated by adding the net global land-use emissions from the CMIP6 scenario database to the other sectoral emissions calculated from climate model runs with prescribed CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> concentrations. <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-016-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-016">33</a></span></sup>Land and ocean CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> uptake since 1850 is calculated from the net biome productivity on land, corrected for CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> losses due to land-use change by adding the land-use change emissions, and net ocean CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> flux.   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">5.2.1; Table 5.1; 5.4.5; Figure 5.25; Box TS.5; Box TS.5, Figure 1</span></span></p><div class="ch-figure-button-cont"><a href="/report/ar6/wg1/figures/summary-for-policymakers/figure-spm-7" target="_blank"><button class="btn-ipcc btn btn-primary ch-figure-button">Open figure</button></a></div></div></div></div><p id="readmore-b5" class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify--all-bold--BLUE--No-space-below readmore"><span class="bulletnum">B.5</span> <span class="readmore bullet-title">Many changes due to past and future greenhouse gas emissions are irreversible for centuries to millennia, especially changes in the ocean, ice sheets and global sea level.</span>      <span class="readmore btn-primary btn-ipcc">Expand</span><span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-8"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.8</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">2.3, Cross-Chapter Box 2.4, 4.3, 4.5, 4.7, 5.3, 9.2, 9.4, 9.5, 9.6, Box 9.4</span></span></p><div class="spmbulletcont" id="spmbulletcont-b5"><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.5.1</span> Past GHG emissions since 1750 have committed the global ocean to future warming (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Over the rest of the 21st century, <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i>ocean warming ranges from 2–4 (SSP1-2.6) to 4–8 times (SSP5-8.5) the 1971–2018 change. Based on multiple lines of evidence, upper ocean stratification (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">virtually certain</i>), ocean acidification (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">virtually certain</i>) and ocean deoxygenation (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>) will continue to increase in the 21st century, at rates dependent on future emissions. Changes are irreversible on centennial to millennial time scales in global ocean temperature (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">very high confidence</i>), deep-ocean acidification (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">very high confidence</i>) and deoxygenation (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>).   <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-8"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.8</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 4.5, 4.7, 5.3, 9.2, TS.2.4</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.5.2</span> Mountain and polar glaciers are committed to continue melting for decades or centuries (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">very high confidence</i>). <i class="•-Condensed-italic"></i>Loss of permafrost carbon following permafrost thaw is irreversible at centennial time scales (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Continued ice loss over the 21st century is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">virtually certain</i> for the Greenland Ice Sheet and <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i> for the Antarctic Ice Sheet. There is <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i> that total ice loss from the Greenland Ice Sheet will increase with cumulative emissions. There is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">limited evidence</i> for low-likelihood, high-impact outcomes (resulting from ice-sheet instability processes characterized by deep uncertainty and in some cases involving tipping points) that would strongly increase ice loss from the Antarctic Ice Sheet for centuries under high GHG emissions scenarios. <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-015-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-015">34</a></span></sup>  <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 4.7, 5.4, 9.4, 9.5, Box 9.4, Box TS.1, TS.2.5</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.5.3</span> It is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">virtually certain</i> that global mean sea level will continue to rise over the 21st century. Relative to 1995–2014, the <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i>global mean sea level rise by 2100 is 0.28–0.55 m under the very low GHG emissions scenario (SSP1-1.9); 0.32–0.62 m under the low GHG emissions scenario (SSP1-2.6); 0.44–0.76 m under the intermediate GHG emissions scenario (SSP2-4.5); and 0.63–1.01 m under the very high GHG emissions scenario (SSP5-8.5); and by 2150 is 0.37–0.86 m under the very low scenario (SSP1-1.9); 0.46–0.99 m under the low scenario (SSP1-2.6); 0.66–1.33 m under the intermediate scenario (SSP2-4.5); and 0.98–1.88 m under the very high scenario (SSP5-8.5) (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-014-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-014">35</a></span></sup>Global mean sea level rise above the <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i>range – approaching 2 m by 2100 and 5 m by 2150 under a very high GHG emissions scenario (SSP5-8.5) (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">low confidence</i>) – cannot be ruled out due to deep uncertainty in ice-sheet processes.   <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-8"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.8</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 9.6, Box 9.4, Box TS.4</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">B.5.4</span> In the longer term, sea level is committed to rise for centuries to millennia due to continuing deep-ocean warming and ice-sheet melt and will remain elevated for thousands of years (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Over the next 2000 years, global mean sea level will rise by about 2 to 3 m if warming is limited to 1.5°C, 2 to 6 m if limited to 2°C and 19 to 22 m with 5°C of warming, and it will continue to rise over subsequent millennia (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">low confidence</i>). Projections of multi-millennial global mean sea level rise are consistent with reconstructed levels during past warm climate periods: <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i>5–10 m higher than today around 125,000 years ago, when global temperatures were <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i>0.5°C–1.5°C higher than 1850–1900; and <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i>5–25 m higher roughly 3 million years ago, when global temperatures were 2.5°C–4°C higher (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">2.3, Cross-Chapter Box 2.4, 9.6, Box TS.2, Box TS.4, Box TS.9</span></span></p><div class="_idGenObjectLayout-1 Body-copy_Boxes_Blue-Boxes_•-Box-extract" id="figure-spm-8"><div class="•-2-column-graphic" id="_idContainer011"><img loading="lazy" alt="" class="_idGenObjectAttribute-1" src="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/figures/IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM_Figure_8.png"/><strong class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-title--bold-to-------spans-columns---Notes-below" lang="en-US"><span class="•-Figure-table-number---title"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.8 | </span> Selected indicators of global climate change under the five illustrative scenarios used in this Report </strong><p class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-table-note---no-title" lang="en-US">The projections for each of the five scenarios are shown in colour. Climate Information for Risk Assessment and Regional Adaptation<span class="share-block"><img class="share-icon" src="../../share.png"/></span></h1><div class="h1-siblings" id="h1-4-siblings"><i class="•-Condensed-italic">Physical climate information addresses how the climate system responds to the interplay between human influence, natural drivers and internal variability. Knowledge of the climate response and the range of possible outcomes, including low-likelihood, high impact outcomes, informs climate services, the assessment of climate-related risks, and adaptation planning. Physical climate information at global, regional and local scales is developed from multiple lines of evidence, including observational products, climate model outputs and tailored diagnostics. </i><p id="readmore-c1" class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify--all-bold--BLUE--No-space-below readmore"><span class="bulletnum">C.1</span> <span class="readmore bullet-title">Natural drivers and internal variability will modulate human-caused changes, especially at regional scales and in the near term, with little effect on centennial global warming. These modulations are important to consider in planning for the full range of possible changes.</span>     <span class="readmore btn-primary btn-ipcc">Expand</span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">1.4, 2.2, 3.3, Cross-Chapter Box 3.1, 4.4, 4.6, Cross-Chapter Box 4.1, Box 7.2, 8.3, 8.5, 9.2, 10.3, 10.4, 10.6, 11.3, 12.5, Atlas.4, Atlas.5, Atlas.8, Atlas.9, Atlas.10, Atlas.11, Cross-Chapter Box Atlas.2</span></span></p><div class="spmbulletcont" id="spmbulletcont-c1"><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.1.1</span> The historical global surface temperature record highlights that decadal variability has both enhanced and masked underlying human-caused long-term changes, and this variability will continue into the future (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">very high confidence</i>). For example, internal decadal variability and variations in solar and volcanic drivers partially masked human-caused surface global warming during 1998–2012, with pronounced regional and seasonal signatures (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Nonetheless, the heating of the climate system continued during this period, as reflected in both the continued warming of the global ocean (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">very high confidence</i>) and in the continued rise of hot extremes over land (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>).    <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-1"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.1</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">1.4, 3.3, Cross-Chapter Box 3.1, 4.4, Box 7.2, 9.2, 11.3, Cross-Section Box TS.1</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.1.2</span> Projected human-caused changes in mean climate and climatic impact-drivers (CIDs), <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-013-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-013">36</a></span></sup> including extremes, will be either amplified or attenuated by internal variability (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-012-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-012">37</a></span></sup>Near-term cooling at any particular location with respect to present climate could occur and would be consistent with the global surface temperature increase due to human influence (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">1.4, 4.4, 4.6, 10.4, 11.3, 12.5, Atlas.5, Atlas.10, Atlas.11, TS.4.2</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.1.3</span> Internal variability has largely been responsible for the amplification and attenuation of the observed human-caused decadal-to-multi-decadal mean precipitation changes in many land regions (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). At global and regional scales, near-term changes in monsoons will be dominated by the effects of internal variability (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). In addition to the influence of internal variability, near-term projected changes in precipitation at global and regional scales are uncertain because of model uncertainty and uncertainty in forcings from natural and anthropogenic aerosols (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">1.4, 4.4, 8.3, 8.5, 10.3, 10.4, 10.5, 10.6, Atlas.4, Atlas.8, Atlas.9, Atlas.10, Atlas.11, Cross-Chapter Box Atlas.2, TS.4.2, Box TS.6, Box TS.13</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify-"><span class="subbullet">C.1.4</span> Based on paleoclimate and historical evidence, it is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i> that at least one large explosive volcanic eruption would occur during the 21st century. <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-011-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-011">38</a></span></sup>Such an eruption would reduce global surface temperature and precipitation, especially over land, for one to three years, alter the global monsoon circulation, modify extreme precipitation and change many CIDs (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). If such an eruption occurs, this would therefore temporarily and partially mask human-caused climate change.   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">2.2, 4.4, Cross-Chapter Box 4.1, 8.5, TS.2.1</span></span></p></div><p id="readmore-c2" class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify--all-bold--BLUE--No-space-below readmore"><span class="bulletnum">C.2</span> <span class="readmore bullet-title">With further global warming, every region is projected to increasingly experience concurrent and multiple changes in climatic impact-drivers. Changes in several climatic impact-drivers would be more widespread at 2°C compared to 1.5°C global warming and even more widespread and/or pronounced for higher warming levels.</span>     <span id="readmore-c2" class="readmore btn-primary btn-ipcc">Expand</span><span class="figure-links"><a href="#table-spm-1"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../table.png"/> Table SPM.1</a> <a href="#figure-spm-9"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.9</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">8.2, 9.3, 9.5, 9.6, Box 10.3, 11.3, 11.4, 11.5, 11.6, 11.7, 11.9, Box 11.3, Box 11.4, Cross-Chapter Box 11.1, 12.2, 12.3, 12.4, 12.5, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, Atlas.4, Atlas.5, Atlas.6, Atlas.7, Atlas.8, Atlas.9, Atlas.10, Atlas.11</span></span></p><div class="spmbulletcont" id="spmbulletcont-c2"><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.2.1</span> All regions<sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-010-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-010">39</a></span></sup> are projected to experience further increases in hot climatic impact-drivers (CIDs) and decreases in cold CIDs (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Further decreases are projected in permafrost; snow, glaciers and ice sheets; and lake and Arctic sea ice (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium</i> to <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i>). <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-009-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-009">40</a></span></sup> These changes would be larger at 2°C global warming or above than at 1.5°C (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). For example, extreme heat thresholds relevant to agriculture and health are projected to be exceeded more frequently at higher global warming levels (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#table-spm-1"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../table.png"/> Table SPM.1</a>    <a href="#figure-spm-9"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.9</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">9.3, 9.5, 11.3, 11.9, Cross-Chapter Box 11.1, 12.3, 12.4, 12.5, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, Atlas.4, Atlas.5, Atlas.6, Atlas.7, Atlas.8, Atlas.9, Atlas.10, Atlas.11, TS.4.3</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.2.2</span> At 1.5°C global warming, heavy precipitation and associated flooding are projected to intensify and be more frequent in most regions in Africa and Asia (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>), North America (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium</i> to <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i>)<sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-009-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-009">40</a></span></sup> and Europe (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). Also, more frequent and/or severe agricultural and ecological droughts are projected in a few regions in all inhabited continents except Asia compared to 1850–1900 (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>); increases in meteorological droughts are also projected in a few regions (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>)<i class="•-Condensed-italic">. </i>A small number of regions are projected to experience increases or decreases in mean precipitation (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>).  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#table-spm-1"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../table.png"/> Table SPM.1</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">11.4, 11.5, 11.6, 11.9, Atlas.4, Atlas.5, Atlas.7, Atlas.8, Atlas.9, Atlas.10, Atlas.11, TS.4.3</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.2.3</span> At 2°C global warming and above, the level of confidence in and the magnitude of the change in droughts and heavy and mean precipitation increase compared to those at 1.5°C. Heavy precipitation and associated flooding events are projected to become more intense and frequent in the Pacific Islands and across many regions of North America and Europe (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium</i> to <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i>).  <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-009-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-009">40</a></span></sup> These changes are also seen in some regions in Australasia and Central and South America (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium  confidence</i>). Several regions in Africa, South America and Europe are projected to experience an increase in frequency and/or severity of agricultural and ecological droughts with <i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium</i> to <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i>;<sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-009-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-009">40</a></span></sup> increases are also projected <i class="•-Condensed-italic"></i> in Australasia, Central and North America, and the Caribbean with <i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>. A small number of regions in Africa, Australasia, Europe and North America are also projected to be affected by increases in hydrological droughts, and several regions are projected to be affected by increases or decreases in meteorological droughts, with more regions displaying an increase (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>)<i class="•-Condensed-italic">. </i>Mean precipitation is projected to increase in all polar, northern European and northern North American regions, most Asian regions and two regions of South America (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#table-spm-1"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../table.png"/> Table SPM.1</a> <a href="#figure-spm-5"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.5</a>,  <a href="#figure-spm-6">Figure SPM.6</a> <a href="#figure-spm-9">Figure SPM.9</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">11.4, 11.6, 11.9, Cross-Chapter Box 11.1, 12.4, 12.5, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, Atlas.5, Atlas.7, Atlas.8, Atlas.9, Atlas.11, TS.4.3</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.2.4</span> More CIDs across more regions are projected to change at 2°C and above compared to 1.5°C global warming (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Region-specific changes include intensification of tropical cyclones and/or extratropical storms (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>), increases in<i class="•-Condensed-italic"></i>river floods (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium</i> to <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i>),  <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-009-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-009">40</a></span></sup> reductions in mean precipitation and increases in aridity (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium</i> to <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i>),  <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-009-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-009">40</a></span></sup> and increases in fire weather (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium</i> to <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i>)<i class="•-Condensed-italic">. </i> <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-009-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-009">40</a></span></sup> There is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">low confidence</i> in most regions in potential future changes in src="../../table.png"/> Table SPM.1</a> <a href="#figure-spm-9"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.9</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">11.7, 11.9, Cross-Chapter Box 11.1, 12.4, 12.5, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, Atlas.4, Atlas.6, Atlas.7, Atlas.8, Atlas.10, TS.4.3.1, TS.4.3.2, TS.5</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.2.5</span> It is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i> to <i class="•-Condensed-italic">virtually certain</i><sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-009-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-009">40</a></span></sup>that regional mean relative sea level rise will continue throughout the 21st century, except in a few regions with substantial geologic land uplift rates. Approximately two-thirds of the global coastline has a projected regional relative sea level rise within ±20% of the global mean increase (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>). Due to relative sea level rise, extreme sea level events that occurred once per century in the recent past are projected to occur at least annually at more than half of all tide gauge locations by 2100 (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Relative sea level rise contributes to increases in the frequency and severity of coastal flooding in low-lying areas and to coastal erosion along most sandy coasts (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-9"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.9</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">9.6, 12.4, 12.5, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, Box TS.4, TS.4.3</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.2.6</span> Cities intensify human-induced warming locally, and further urbanization together with more frequent hot extremes will increase the severity of heatwaves (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">very high confidence</i>). Urbanization also increases mean and heavy precipitation over and/or downwind of cities (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i>) and resulting runoff intensity (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). In coastal cities, the combination of more frequent extreme sea level events (due to sea level rise and storm surge) and extreme rainfall/riverflow events will make flooding more probable (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">8.2, Box 10.3, 11.3, 12.4, Box TS.14</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.2.7</span> Many regions are projected to experience an increase in the probability of compound events with higher global warming (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). In particular, concurrent heatwaves and droughts are <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i> to become more frequent. Concurrent extremes at multiple locations, including in crop-producing areas, become more frequent at 2°C and above compared to 1.5°C global warming (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#table-spm-1"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../table.png"/> Table SPM.1</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">11.8, Box 11.3, Box 11.4, 12.3, 12.4, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, TS.4.3</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify- _idGenParaOverride-1"></p><div class="_idGenObjectLayout-1 Body-copy_Boxes_Blue-Boxes_•-Box-extract" id="figure-spm-9"><div class="•-2-column-graphic" id="_idContainer012"><img loading="lazy" alt="" class="_idGenObjectAttribute-1" src="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/figures/IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM_Figure_9.png"/><p><strong class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-title--bold-to-------spans-columns---Notes-below" lang="en-US"><span class="•-Figure-table-number---title"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.9 | </span> Synthesis of the number of AR6 WGI reference regions where climatic impact-drivers are projected to change</strong></p><p class="Body-copy_Figures--tables-etc_•-Figure-table-note---no-title" lang="en-US">A total of 35 climatic impact-drivers (CIDs) grouped into seven types are shown: heat and cold; wet and dry; wind; snow and ice; coastal; open ocean; and other. 4.8, Cross-Chapter Box 4.1, 8.6, 9.2, Box 9.4, 11.8, Box 11.2, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1</span></span></p><div class="spmbulletcont" id="spmbulletcont-c3"><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.3.1</span> If global warming exceeds the assessed <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i>range <i class="•-Condensed-italic"></i> for a given GHG emissions scenario, including low GHG emissions scenarios, global and regional changes in many aspects of the climate system, such as regional precipitation and other CIDs, would also exceed their assessed <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i>ranges (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Such low-likelihood, high-warming outcomes are associated with potentially very large impacts, such as through more intense and more frequent heatwaves and heavy precipitation, and high risks for human and ecological systems, particularly for high GHG emissions scenarios.  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#table-spm-1"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../table.png"/> Table SPM.1</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">Cross-Chapter Box 1.3, 4.3, 4.4, 4.8, Box 9.4, Box 11.2, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, TS.1.4, Box TS.3, Box TS.4</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.3.2</span> Low-likelihood, high-impact outcomes<sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-015-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-015">34</a></span></sup>could occur at global and regional scales even for global warming within the <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i>range for a given GHG emissions scenario. The probability of low-likelihood, high-impact outcomes increases with higher global warming levels (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>). Abrupt responses and tipping points of the climate system, such as strongly increased Antarctic ice-sheet melt and forest dieback, cannot be ruled out (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#table-spm-1"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../table.png"/> Table SPM.1</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">1.4, 4.3, 4.4, 4.8, 5.4, 8.6, Box 9.4, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, TS.1.4, TS.2.5, Box TS.3, Box TS.4, Box TS.9</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.3.3</span> If global warming increases, some compound extreme events<sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- _idGenCharOverride-1"><span id="footnote-031-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-031">18</a></span></sup> with low likelihood in past and current climate will become more frequent, and there will be a higher likelihood that events with increased intensities, durations and/or spatial extents unprecedented in the observational record will occur (<i class="•-Condensed-italic">high confidence</i>).   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">11.8, Box 11.2, Cross-Chapter Box 12.1, Box TS.3, Box TS.9</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.3.4</span> The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i> to weaken over the 21st century for all emissions scenarios. While there is <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i> in the 21st century decline, there is only<i class="•-Condensed-italic">low confidence</i> in the magnitude of the trend. There is <i class="•-Condensed-italic">medium confidence</i> that there will not be an abrupt collapse before 2100. If such a collapse were to occur, it would <i class="•-Condensed-italic">very likely </i>cause abrupt shifts in regional weather patterns and water cycle, such as a southward shift in the tropical rain belt, weakening of the African and Asian monsoons and strengthening of Southern Hemisphere monsoons, and drying in Europe.   <span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">4.3, 8.6, 9.2, TS2.4, Box TS.3</span></span></p><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">C.3.5</span> Unpredictable and rare natural events not related to human influence on climate may lead to low-likelihood, high-impact outcomes. For example, a sequence of large explosive volcanic eruptions within decades has occurred in the past, causing substantial global and regional climate perturbations over several decades. Such events cannot be ruled out in the future, but due to their inherent unpredictability they are not included in the illustrative set of scenarios referred to in this Report  <span class="figure-links"><a href="#box-spm-1"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../box.png"/> Box SPM.1</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">2.2, Cross-Chapter Box 4.1, Box TS.3</span></span></p></div></div></div><div class="h1-container" id="D."><h1 class="SPM-Summary-for-Policymakers-styles_•-SPM-Introduction-head---no-space-below ParaOverride-4">D. Limiting Future Climate Change<span class="share-block"><img class="share-icon" src="../../share.png"/></span></h1><div class="h1-siblings" id="h1-5-siblings"><i class="•-Condensed-italic">Since AR5, estimates of remaining carbon budgets have been improved by a new methodology first presented in SR1.5, updated evidence, and the integration of results from multiple lines of evidence. A comprehensive range of possible future air pollution controls in scenarios is used to consistently assess the effects of various assumptions on projections of climate and air pollution. A novel development is the ability to ascertain when climate responses to emissions reductions would become discernible above natural climate variability, including internal variability and responses to natural drivers. </i><p id="readmore-d1" class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify--all-bold--BLUE--No-space-below readmore"><span class="bulletnum">D.1</span> <span class="readmore bullet-title">From a physical science perspective, limiting human-induced global warming to a specific level requires limiting cumulative CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions, reaching at least net zero CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">2</sub> emissions, along with strong reductions in other greenhouse gas emissions. Strong, rapid and sustained reductions in CH<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- _idGenCharOverride-1">4</sub> emissions would also limit the warming effect resulting from declining aerosol pollution and would improve air quality.</span> <span id="readmore-d1" class="readmore btn-primary btn-ipcc">Expand</span><span class="figure-links"><a href="#figure-spm-10"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../chart.png"/> Figure SPM.10</a> <a href="#table-spm-2"><img loading="lazy" class="chart-icon" src="../../table.png"/> Table SPM.2</a></span><span><span class="ch-link">Links to chapters</span><span class="ch-link-popup">3.3, 4.6, 5.1, 5.2, 5.4, 5.5, 5.6, Box 5.2, Cross-Chapter Box 5.1, 6.7, 7.6, 9.6</span></span></p><div class="spmbulletcont" id="spmbulletcont-d1"><p class="Body-copy_•-Body-copy--full-justify----no-space-below"><span class="subbullet">D.1.1</span> This Report reaffirms with <i class="•-Condensed-italic"> high confidence</i> the AR5 finding that there is a near-linear relationship between cumulative anthropogenic CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- CharOverride-2">2</sub> emissions and the global warming they cause. Each 1000 GtCO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- CharOverride-2">2</sub> of cumulative CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- CharOverride-2">2</sub> emissions is assessed to <i class="•-Condensed-italic">likely </i>cause a 0.27°C to 0.63°C increase in global surface temperature with a best estimate of 0.45°C. <sup class="•-Superscript--e-g--footnote-refs-in-text- CharOverride-2"><span id="footnote-008-backlink"><a class="_idFootnoteLink _idGenColorInherit" href="spm.html#footnote-008">41</a></span></sup> This is a narrower range compared to AR5 and SR1.5. This quantity is referred to as the transient climate response to cumulative CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- CharOverride-2">2</sub> emissions (TCRE). This relationship implies that reaching net zero anthropogenic CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- CharOverride-2">2</sub> emissions<span class="CharOverride-9"><span any level, but that limiting global temperature increase to a specific level would imply limiting cumulative CO<sub class="•-Subscript--e-g--for-CO2-etc- CharOverride-2">2</sub> emissions to within a
